newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: WOLFF WARNS ON POTENTIAL EL NINO METALS DISRUPTION.
newsitem.headline: WOLFF WARNS ON POTENTIAL EL NINO METALS DISRUPTION.

text.p: The El Nino weather phenomenon had the potential to disrupt supplies in a generally bullish base metals market, London Metal Exchange (LME) trader Rudolf Wolff & Co said on Tuesday.
Rudolf Wolff analyst William Adams said the biggest impact would be on copper, either through heavy rains in South America or drought in Australia and neighbouring countries.

"The weather patterns are set to change at around the end of the year so we should brace ourselves to expect more supply and transportation disruptions," Adams told a Bell Securities Ltd base metals conference here.

The effect of weather on copper had been seen earlier in the year when lack of rain lowered water levels in the Fly River in Papua New Guinea, disrupting supplies from The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd's Ok Tedi mine, he said.

Up to 60 percent of world copper output had the potential to be disrupted by El Nino, a weather condition caused by warming of water in the western Pacific Ocean which creates drought in some areas and heavier-than-normal rainfall in others.
This compared with about 46 percent of nickel production and about 37 percent of zinc production.
Adams said heavy rains could also affect solvent extraction/electrowinning copper operations in South America, by diluting pools used for solvent extraction.
"It is also transport, because with flooding rail lines can be washed away, embankments can be washed away and there can be landslides," he added.
Adams said Wolff was bearish on copper, forecasting stock increases, but was bullish on aluminium, zinc and nickel, where stocks were likely to fall.
LME aluminium stocks had fallen about 30 percent in 1997.
Total commercial stocks stood at about 6.3 weeks worth of production and were expected to fall to about 5.2 weeks in 1998.

Adams said aluminium producers were likely to lift production if faced with increasing substitution from PET bottles, but investment interest from funds and other financial institutions should absorb producer selling.
Zinc fundamentals should tighten, cutting stocks from 6.7 weeks of production at present to below three weeks over the next two years.
Adams said zinc had been in the doldrums for so long that there had been little new investment in production.
Prices had already run up as current stocks were tightly held and some consumers had been under-hedged.
In general, base metal prices were likely to benefit from good economic growth in the U.S., a more confident Europe and recovery in Japan.
